summary: Suggests a simple method for workstations to dynamically access mail from a mailbox server. It describes Post Office Protocol version 3 and was on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 1460.

eli5.summary: Your mail waits at a post office. This is how your computer asks to pick it up.

how do you authenticate in pop3
subtitle: How lightweight workstations retrieve mail from a server without running their own mail system.

tldr.problem: Workstations and personal computers often lack the resources to run a full mail transport system, so they need a simple way to retrieve mail that a server is holding for them.
tldr.mechanism: POP3 lets a client authenticate with a username and password, then download messages from a server mailbox using simple commands, optionally marking them for deletion before disconnecting.
tldr.outcome: The protocol became the standard way for lightweight email clients to retrieve mail. It was later improved by RFC 1460, and split-UA architecture (combining SMTP for sending and POP3 for receiving) remains common today.

facts.value: 10 (USER, PASS, STAT, LIST, RETR, DELE, NOOP, LAST, RSET, QUIT)

today: RFC 1225 was obsoleted by RFC 1460 in 1993. The POP3 protocol lives on in modern email clients, though newer protocols like IMAP offer more features for users who want to keep mail on the server. The split-UA model—where a client uses SMTP to send and POP3 or IMAP to receive—is still the standard architecture for lightweight email clients.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Personal computers and lightweight workstations often cannot spare the disk space or CPU cycles to run a full message transport system (MTS) like SMTP. Yet users on these machines still want to read their mail. POP3 (Post Office Protocol Version 3) solves this by letting small clients retrieve mail that a server is holding for them, without the small machine having to run its own mail infrastructure.

The protocol is transaction-oriented: a client connects, authenticates, downloads its messages, optionally marks some for deletion, and disconnects. The trade-off is simplicity—POP3 does not offer the rich message management that a full MTS does, but it is small enough to implement on any computer.
sections.eli5: Your mail waits at a post office instead of your home mailbox. When you want it, you go in, show your ID, pick up your messages, decide which ones to throw away, and leave. The post office cleans up the trash when you leave.

sections.title: How a POP3 Session Works
sections.content:
A POP3 client connects to a POP3 server on TCP port 110. The connection moves through three states.

Authorization state: The server sends a greeting. The client sends a USER command with a username, and if the server accepts it, sends a PASS command with a password. If authentication succeeds, the server locks the user's mailbox and the session enters the transaction state.

Transaction state: The client can now issue commands to list, retrieve, and delete messages. The STAT command returns the number and total size of messages. LIST shows message IDs and sizes. RETR retrieves a full message. DELE marks a message for deletion. Optional commands like TOP retrieve just the headers and a few lines of body. The LAST command tells the client which message number it last accessed, so it can retrieve only new mail on the next session.

Update state: When the client sends QUIT, the server permanently deletes all messages marked for deletion, releases the mailbox lock, and closes the connection.
sections.eli5: Step one: you prove who you are. Step two: you list your mail, read what you want, mark some for removal. Step three: you say goodbye, and the post office throws away what you marked and closes the door.

sections.title: Commands and Message Handling
sections.content:
POP3 commands are simple: a keyword and optional arguments, followed by CRLF. Responses are a status indicator (+OK for success, -ERR for failure), possibly followed by data.

Messages are sent as multi-line responses: after the status line, the server sends the message content, then a line with a single dot and CRLF to mark the end. If a message line starts with a dot, the server prefixes an extra dot (byte-stuffing) so the client knows it is not the end marker. The client reverses this when reading.

Message sizes in the RFC are always in octets (bytes), and the server counts lines in local representation (for example, converting single newline characters to CRLF pairs for the octet count). The client can calculate the true octet size based on how the server represents line endings.

All messages are assumed to follow the RFC 822 mail message format (headers, blank line, body), but POP3 does not parse them—it just moves bytes.
sections.eli5: Messages are sent one line at a time. If a line happens to start with a dot (like a real dot-point in the message), the server adds an extra dot so you know it is not the end signal. You remove that extra dot when you read it.

sections.title: The Split-UA Model
sections.content:
POP3 is designed for a split-UA (user agent) architecture. A traditional user agent handles both sending (via SMTP) and receiving (via a local mailbox). In the split-UA model, the user agent is split across two machines: the lightweight client posts mail via SMTP to a relay host (often the same server that holds its mailbox), and retrieves mail via POP3 from a mail server.

This works because the client does not need to be a trusted mail server itself. When the client connects to SMTP, the server treats it as an untrusted user agent and validates the message. When it connects to POP3, it authenticates with a password and can only access its own mailbox.

The RFC notes that other transport mechanisms besides TCP/IP could carry POP3 (such as dial-up terminal sessions), and that some implementations do not require password authentication if they rely on a lower-level login session or trusted network authentication.
sections.eli5: Instead of your computer being a full post office, it is just a customer. You send letters to the post office's SMTP dock, and you pick up your mail from the POP3 window. Two separate services, one machine.

sections.title: Minimal and Optional Commands
sections.content:
All POP3 servers must support the minimal command set: USER, PASS, STAT, LIST, RETR, DELE, NOOP, LAST, RSET, and QUIT. The NOOP command does nothing and is useful only to keep a connection alive. The RSET command clears all deletion marks and resets the LAST position.

Optional commands let advanced servers offer more features without burdening minimal implementations. TOP lets the client retrieve just the headers and a few lines of body (useful for previewing large messages). RPOP is an authentication method using host-level credentials for trusted networks—the RFC warns that this method has been widely exploited for unauthorized access.

The RFC strongly discourages servers from adding extra information to responses unless clients ask for it via optional commands. The philosophy is to keep servers simple and put intelligence in the client.
sections.eli5: A basic post office window has ten things it can do. Fancy post offices can do more, but you never have to ask for the fancy stuff. The smart clients ask for only what they need.
